pages.caption: Once upon a time there dwelt on the outskirts of a large forest a poor
woodcutter with his wife and two children; the boy was called Hansel and the girl
Grettel.
He had always little enough to live on, and once, when there was a great
famine in the land, he couldn't even provide them with daily bread.
One night, as he was tossing about in bed, full of cares and worry, he
pages.description: [establishing shot of worried father in bed]

pages.caption: sighed and said to his wife: "What's to become of us? how are we to
pages.description: [close-up detail of worried father in bed]

pages.caption: support our poor children, now that we have nothing more for ourselves?"
"I'll tell you what, husband," answered the woman; "early to-morrow morning we'll take the children
pages.description: [establishing shot of cruel stepmother hatching plan]

pages.caption: out into the thickest part of the wood; there we shall light a fire for
pages.description: [close-up detail of cruel stepmother hatching plan]

pages.caption: them and give them each a piece of bread; then we'll go on to our
work and leave them alone.
pages.description: [wide view of cruel stepmother hatching plan]

pages.caption: They won't be able to find their way home, and we shall thus be rid
of them." "No, wife," said her husband, "that I won't do; how could I find
it in my heart to leave my children alone in the wood?
The wild beasts would soon come and tear them to pieces." "Oh! you fool," said
pages.description: [establishing shot of wild beasts threatening in darkness]

pages.caption: she,
pages.description: [close-up detail of wild beasts threatening in darkness]

pages.caption: "then we must all four die of hunger, and you may just as well go
pages.description: [characters in wild beasts threatening in darkness]

pages.caption: and plane the boards for our coffins"; and she left him no peace till he
pages.description: [wide view of wild beasts threatening in darkness]

pages.caption: consented.
pages.description: [intimate moment in wild beasts threatening in darkness]

pages.caption: "But I can't help feeling sorry for the poor children," added the husband.
pages.description: [establishing shot of sad father holding his head]

pages.caption: The children, too, had not been able to sleep for hunger, and had heard what
pages.description: [establishing shot of children whispering in moonlit room]

pages.caption: their step-mother had said to their father.
pages.description: [close-up detail of children whispering in moonlit room]

pages.caption: Grettel wept bitterly and spoke to Hansel: "Now it's all up with us."
"No, no, Grettel," said Hansel, "don't fret yourself; I'll be able to find a way
to escape,
no fear."
And when the old people had fallen asleep he got up, slipped on his little
pages.description: [establishing shot of hansel gathering white pebbles]

pages.caption: coat,
pages.description: [close-up detail of hansel gathering white pebbles]

pages.caption: opened the back door and stole out. The moon was shining clearly, and the white
pebbles which lay in front of the house glittered like bits of silver.
pages.description: [wide view of hansel gathering white pebbles]

pages.caption: Hansel bent down and filled his pocket with as many of them as he could
pages.description: [establishing shot of white pebbles in pockets]

pages.caption: cram in.
pages.description: [close-up detail of white pebbles in pockets]

pages.caption: Then he went back and said to Grettel: "Be comforted, my dear little sister, and
pages.description: [establishing shot of hansel whispering to sister]

pages.caption: go to sleep: God will not desert us"; and he lay down in bed again.
pages.description: [close-up detail of hansel whispering to sister]

pages.caption: At daybreak, even before the sun was up, the woman came and woke the two
pages.description: [establishing shot of stepmother waking children at dawn]

pages.caption: children:
pages.description: [close-up detail of stepmother waking children at dawn]

pages.caption: "Get up, you lie-abeds, we're all going to the forest to fetch wood."
pages.description: [characters in stepmother waking children at dawn]

pages.caption: She gave them each a bit of bread and said: "There's something for your luncheon,
pages.description: [establishing shot of small piece of bread]

pages.caption: but don't you eat it up before, for it's all you'll get."
pages.description: [close-up detail of small piece of bread]

pages.caption: Grettel took the bread under her apron, as Hansel had the stones in his pocket.
pages.description: [establishing shot of children following into forest]

pages.caption: Then they all set out together on the way to the forest.
pages.description: [close-up detail of children following into forest]

pages.caption: After they had walked for a little, Hansel stood still and looked back at the
pages.description: [establishing shot of hansel looking back repeatedly]

pages.caption: house,
pages.description: [close-up detail of hansel looking back repeatedly]

pages.caption: and this maneuver he repeated again and again.
His father observed him, and said: "Hansel, what are you gazing at there, and why
do you always remain behind? Take care, and don't lose your footing."
"Oh! father," said Hansel, "I am looking back at my white kitten, which is sitting
pages.description: [establishing shot of hansel pointing at roof]

pages.caption: on the roof, waving me a farewell."
pages.description: [close-up detail of hansel pointing at roof]

pages.caption: The woman exclaimed: "What a donkey you are! that isn't your kitten, that's the morning
sun shining on the chimney."
But Hansel had not looked back at his kitten, but had always dropped one of
pages.description: [establishing shot of white pebble dropping on path]

pages.caption: the white pebbles out of his pocket on to the path.
pages.description: [close-up detail of white pebble dropping on path]

pages.caption: When they had reached the middle of the forest the father said: "Now, children, go
and fetch a lot of wood, and I'll light a fire that you may not
feel cold."
Hansel and Grettel heaped up brushwood till they had made a pile nearly the size
pages.description: [establishing shot of huge pile of brushwood]

pages.caption: of a small hill.
pages.description: [close-up detail of huge pile of brushwood]

pages.caption: The brushwood was set fire to, and when the flames leaped high the woman said:
"Now lie down at the fire, children, and rest yourselves: we are going into the
forest to cut down wood; when we've finished we'll come back and fetch you."
Hansel and Grettel sat down beside the fire, and at midday ate their little bits
pages.description: [establishing shot of children sleeping by fire]

pages.caption: of bread.
pages.description: [close-up detail of children sleeping by fire]

pages.caption: They heard the strokes of the axe, so they thought their father was quite near.
pages.description: [establishing shot of bough tied to dead tree]

pages.caption: But it was no axe they heard, but a bough he had tied on a
pages.description: [close-up detail of bough tied to dead tree]

pages.caption: dead tree,
pages.description: [characters in bough tied to dead tree]

pages.caption: and that was blown about by the wind.
pages.description: [wide view of bough tied to dead tree]

pages.caption: And when they had sat for a long time their eyes closed with fatigue, and
pages.description: [establishing shot of children waking in darkness]

pages.caption: they fell fast asleep. When they awoke at last it was pitch dark.
pages.description: [close-up detail of children waking in darkness]

pages.caption: Grettel began to cry, and said: "How are we ever to get out of the
pages.description: [establishing shot of grettel crying in darkness]

pages.caption: wood?"
pages.description: [close-up detail of grettel crying in darkness]

pages.caption: But Hansel comforted her. "Wait a bit," he said, "till the moon is up, and
pages.description: [establishing shot of hansel pointing at moon]

pages.caption: then we'll find our way sure enough."
pages.description: [close-up detail of hansel pointing at moon]

pages.caption: And when the full moon had risen he took his sister by the hand and
followed the pebbles, which shone like new threepenny bits, and showed them the path.
They walked on through the night, and at daybreak reached their father's house again. They
knocked at the door, and when the woman opened it she exclaimed: "You naughty children,
what a time you've slept in the wood! we thought you were never going to
come back."
But the father rejoiced, for his conscience had reproached him for leaving his children behind
by themselves.
Not long afterward there was again great dearth in the land, and the children heard
their mother address their father thus in bed one night: "Everything is eaten up once
more;
we have only half a loaf in the house, and when that's done it's all
up with us.
The children must be got rid of; we'll lead them deeper into the wood this
time,
so that they won't be able to find their way out again. There is no
other way of saving ourselves."
The man's heart smote him heavily, and he thought: "Surely it would be better to
share the last bite with one's children!" But his wife wouldn't listen to his arguments,
and did nothing but scold and reproach him.
But the children were awake, and had heard the conversation. When the old people were
asleep Hansel got up, and wanted to go out and pick up pebbles again, as
he had done the first time; but the woman had barred the door, and Hansel
couldn't get out.
But he consoled his little sister, and said: "Don't cry, Grettel, and sleep peacefully, for
God is sure to help us."
At early dawn the woman came and made the children get up. They received their
pages.description: [establishing shot of stepmother giving tiny bread]

pages.caption: bit of bread, but it was even smaller than the time before.
pages.description: [close-up detail of stepmother giving tiny bread]

pages.caption: On the way to the wood Hansel crumbled it in his pocket, and every few
minutes he stood still and dropped a crumb on the ground.
"Hansel, what are you stopping and looking about you for?" said the father.
"I'm looking back at my little pigeon, which is sitting on the roof waving me
pages.description: [establishing shot of hansel pointing at pigeon]

pages.caption: a farewell," answered Hansel.
pages.description: [close-up detail of hansel pointing at pigeon]

pages.caption: "Fool!" said the wife; "that isn't your pigeon, it's the morning sun glittering on the
chimney."
But Hansel gradually threw all his crumbs on the path.
The woman led the children still deeper into the forest farther than they had ever
been in their lives before.
Then a big fire was lit again, and the mother said: "Just sit down there,
pages.description: [establishing shot of fire and mother leaving]

pages.caption: children, and if you're tired you can sleep a bit; we're going into the forest
pages.description: [close-up detail of fire and mother leaving]

pages.caption: to cut down wood, and in the evening when we're finished we'll come back to
fetch you."
pages.description: [wide view of fire and mother leaving]

pages.caption: At midday Grettel divided her bread with Hansel, for he had strewn his all along
their path.
Then they fell asleep, and evening passed away, but nobody came to the poor children.
They didn't awake till it was pitch dark, and Hansel comforted his sister, saying: "Only
wait,
Grettel, till the moon rises, then we shall see the bread-crumbs I scattered along the
path;
they will show us the way back to the house."
When the moon appeared they got up, but they found no crumbs, for the thousands
pages.description: [establishing shot of no crumbs on path]

pages.caption: of birds that fly about the woods and fields had picked them all up.
pages.description: [close-up detail of no crumbs on path]

pages.caption: "Never mind," said Hansel to Grettel; "you'll see we'll find a way out"; but all
the same they did not. They wandered about the whole night, and the next day,
from morning till evening, but they could not find a path out of the wood.
They were very hungry, too, for they had nothing to eat but a few berries
they found growing on the ground.
And at last they were so tired that their legs refused to carry them any
pages.description: [establishing shot of children exhausted under tree]

pages.caption: longer,
pages.description: [close-up detail of children exhausted under tree]

pages.caption: so they lay down under a tree and fell fast asleep.
On the third morning after they had left their father's house they set about their
pages.description: [establishing shot of white bird on branch]

pages.caption: wandering again,
pages.description: [close-up detail of white bird on branch]

pages.caption: but only got deeper and deeper into the wood, and now they felt that if
help did not come to them soon they must perish. At midday they saw a
pages.description: [wide view of white bird on branch]

pages.caption: beautiful little snow-white bird sitting on a branch, which sang so sweetly that they stopped
pages.description: [intimate moment in white bird on branch]

pages.caption: still and listened to it.
pages.description: [dramatic angle of white bird on branch]

pages.caption: And when its song was finished it flapped its wings and flew on in front
pages.description: [establishing shot of bird leading to cottage]

pages.caption: of them.
pages.description: [close-up detail of bird leading to cottage]

pages.caption: They followed it and came to a little house, on the roof of which it
perched.
pages.description: [wide view of bird leading to cottage]

pages.caption: And when they came quite near they saw that the cottage was made of bread
pages.description: [establishing shot of bread house with candy windows]

pages.caption: and roofed with cakes, while the window was made of transparent sugar.
pages.description: [close-up detail of bread house with candy windows]

pages.caption: "Now we'll set to," said Hansel, "and have a regular blow-out. I'll eat a bit
pages.description: [establishing shot of children eating the house]

pages.caption: of the roof, and you, Grettel, can eat some of the window, which you'll find
pages.description: [close-up detail of children eating the house]

pages.caption: a sweet morsel."
Hansel stretched up his hand and broke off a little bit of the roof to
see what it was like, and Grettel went to the casement and began to nibble
at it.
Thereupon a shrill voice called out from the room inside: "Nibble, nibble, little mouse, Who's
nibbling my house?"
The children answered: "Tis Heaven's own child, The tempest wild," and went on eating, without
putting themselves about.
Hansel, who thoroughly appreciated the roof, tore down a big bit of it, while Grettel
pages.description: [establishing shot of grettel pushing out window]

pages.caption: pushed out a whole round window-pane, and sat down the better to enjoy it.
pages.description: [close-up detail of grettel pushing out window]

pages.caption: Suddenly the door opened, and an ancient dame leaning on a staff hobbled out. Hansel
and Grettel were so terrified that they let what they had in their hands fall.
But the old woman shook her head and said: "Oh, ho! you dear children, who
led you here? Just come in and stay with me, no ill shall befall you."
She took them both by the hand and let them into the house, and laid
a most sumptuous dinner before them--milk and sugared pancakes, with apples and nuts.
After they had finished, two beautiful little white beds were prepared for them, and when
pages.description: [establishing shot of children in white beds]

pages.caption: Hansel and Grettel lay down in them they felt as if they had got into
pages.description: [close-up detail of children in white beds]

pages.caption: heaven.
The old woman had appeared to be most friendly, but she was really an old
pages.description: [establishing shot of witch revealing true nature]

pages.caption: witch who had waylaid the children, and had only built the little bread house in
pages.description: [close-up detail of witch revealing true nature]

pages.caption: order to lure them in.
When anyone came into her power she killed, cooked, and ate him, and held a
regular feast-day for the occasion. Now witches have red eyes, and cannot see far, but,
like beasts, they have a keen sense of smell, and know when human beings pass
by.
When Hansel and Grettel fell into her hands she laughed maliciously, and said jeeringly: "I've
got them now; they sha'n't escape me."
Early in the morning, before the children were awake, she rose up, and when she
pages.description: [establishing shot of hansel locked in stable]

pages.caption: saw them both sleeping so peacefully, with their round rosy cheeks, she muttered to herself:
pages.description: [close-up detail of hansel locked in stable]

pages.caption: "That'll be a dainty bite." Then she seized Hansel with her bony hand and carried
him into a little stable, and barred the door on him; he might scream as
pages.description: [wide view of hansel locked in stable]

pages.caption: much as he liked, it did him no good.
pages.description: [intimate moment in hansel locked in stable]

pages.caption: Then she went to Grettel, shook her till she awoke, and cried: "Get up, you
pages.description: [establishing shot of grettel forced to work]

pages.caption: lazy-bones,
pages.description: [close-up detail of grettel forced to work]

pages.caption: fetch water and cook something for your brother. When he's fat I'll eat him up."
Grettel began to cry bitterly, but it was of no use; she had to do
what the wicked witch bade her.
So the best food was cooked for poor Hansel, but Grettel got nothing but crab-shells.
pages.description: [establishing shot of hansel fed, grettel starved]

pages.caption: Every morning the old woman hobbled out to the stable and cried: "Hansel, put out
your finger,
that I may feel if you are getting fat."
But Hansel always stretched out a bone, and the old dame, whose eyes were dim,
pages.description: [establishing shot of hansel holding out bone]

pages.caption: couldn't see it, and thinking always it was Hansel's finger, wondered why he fattened so
pages.description: [close-up detail of hansel holding out bone]

pages.caption: slowly.
When four weeks had passed and Hansel still remained thin, she lost patience and determined
to wait no longer. "Hi, Grettel," she called to the girl, "be quick and get
some water.
Hansel may be fat or thin, I'm going to kill him to-morrow and cook him."
Oh! how the poor little sister sobbed as she carried the water, and how the
tears rolled down her cheeks! "Kind heaven help us now!" she cried; "if only the
wild beasts in the wood had eaten us, then at least we should have died
together."
"Just hold your peace," said the old hag; "it won't help you."
Early in the morning Grettel had to go out and hang up the kettle full
pages.description: [establishing shot of oven blazing with fire]

pages.caption: of water,
pages.description: [close-up detail of oven blazing with fire]

pages.caption: and light the fire. "First we'll bake," said the old dame; "I've heated the oven
already and kneaded the dough."
pages.description: [wide view of oven blazing with fire]

pages.caption: She pushed Grettel out to the oven, from which fiery flames were already issuing. "Creep
pages.description: [establishing shot of witch pushing toward oven]

pages.caption: in," said the witch, "and see if it's properly heated, so that we can shove
pages.description: [close-up detail of witch pushing toward oven]

pages.caption: in the bread."
For when she had got Grettel in she meant to close the oven and let
the girl bake, that she might eat her up too. But Grettel perceived her intention,
and said: "I don't know how I'm to do it; how do I get in?"
"You silly goose!" said the hag, "the opening is big enough; see, I could get
in myself," and she crawled toward it, and poked her head into the oven.
Then Grettel gave her a shove that sent her right in, shut the iron door,
and drew the bolt.
Gracious! how she yelled, it was quite horrible; but Grettel fled, and the wretched old
pages.description: [establishing shot of witch burning in oven]

pages.caption: woman was left to perish miserably.
pages.description: [close-up detail of witch burning in oven]

pages.caption: Grettel flew straight to Hansel, opened the little stable-door, and cried: "Hansel, we are free;
the old witch is dead."
Then Hansel sprang like a bird out of a cage when the door is opened.
How they rejoiced, and fell on each other's necks, and jumped for joy, and kissed
one another!
And as they had no longer any cause for fear, they went in the old
pages.description: [establishing shot of hidden treasure in cottage]

pages.caption: hag's house,
pages.description: [close-up detail of hidden treasure in cottage]

pages.caption: and here they found, in every corner of the room, boxes with pearls and precious
stones.
pages.description: [wide view of hidden treasure in cottage]

pages.caption: "These are even better than pebbles," said Hansel, and crammed his pockets full of them;
and Grettel said: "I too will bring something home," and she filled her apron full.
"But now," said Hansel, "let's go and get well away from the witch's wood." When
pages.description: [establishing shot of leaving the witch's wood]

pages.caption: they had wandered about for some hours they came to a big lake.
pages.description: [close-up detail of leaving the witch's wood]

pages.caption: "We can't get over," said Hansel; "I see no bridge of any sort or kind."
pages.description: [establishing shot of children at water's edge]

pages.caption: "Yes,
pages.description: [close-up detail of children at water's edge]

pages.caption: and there's no ferry-boat either," answered Grettel; "but look, there swims a white duck; if
I ask her she'll help us over," and she called out:
pages.description: [wide view of children at water's edge]

pages.caption: "Here are two children, mournful very, Seeing neither bridge nor ferry; Take us upon your
pages.description: [establishing shot of calling to white duck]

pages.caption: white back,
pages.description: [close-up detail of calling to white duck]

pages.caption: And row us over, quack, quack!"
The duck swam toward them, and Hansel got on her back and bade his little
sister sit beside him.
"No," answered Grettel, "we should be too heavy a load for the duck: she shall
pages.description: [establishing shot of grettel on separate trip]

pages.caption: carry us across separately." The good bird did this, and when they were landed safely
pages.description: [close-up detail of grettel on separate trip]

pages.caption: on the other side, and had gone for a while, the wood became more and
more familiar to them.
pages.description: [wide view of grettel on separate trip]

pages.caption: At length they saw their father's house in the distance. Then they set off to
run,
and bounding into the room fell on their father's neck.
The man had not passed a happy hour since he left them in the wood,
but the woman had died.
Grettel shook out her apron so that the pearls and precious stones rolled about the
room,
and Hansel threw down one handful after the other out of his pocket.
Thus all their troubles were ended, and they lived happily ever afterward.
My story is done. See! there runs a little mouse; anyone who catches it may
make himself a large fur cap out of it.
